nameStory: The name 'scup' comes from the Narragansett Indian word 'mishcuppauog,' which was shortened by early colonists. This fish is also widely called 'porgy,' a name it shares with many relatives in the seabream family, making scup part of New England's rich Native American fishing heritage.
description: Scup are silvery, deep-bodied fish with a compressed, oval shape that makes them look like they've been flattened from the sides. These members of the porgy family typically weigh between half a pound to one pound, though the largest can reach 18 inches and weigh up to 4 pounds. They're one of New England's most important coastal fish, swimming in schools along our shores from spring through fall. With their shimmering scales and distinctive profile, scup are easily recognizable once you know what to look for.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Deep, laterally compressed oval body that feels firm and muscular when handled, like a silvery dinner plate turned on its side

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright silvery sides with a slightly darker back, scales feel smooth and slippery with a metallic sheen that catches sunlight

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single dorsal fin with sharp spiny rays in front and softer rays behind, pectoral fins feel strong and pointed

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small terminal mouth with thick lips and strong teeth that you can feel if you run your finger along the jaw

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Most commonly 8-12 inches long and weighing about the same as a can of soda, though large ones can reach 18 inches

habitat: Scup inhabit coastal waters from sandy beaches to rocky bottoms, preferring areas with mixed sand and vegetation where they can forage. You'll find them in harbors, bays, and along the continental shelf, often in schools near structure like reefs, wrecks, or jetties. They favor waters with good current flow and are commonly found in depths ranging from shallow tide pools to deeper offshore waters.

seasonality.spring: Scup begin their inshore migration as water temperatures warm, appearing in increasing numbers along beaches and in harbors. This is when you'll start seeing them in shallow waters after their winter offshore retreat.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for scup, when they're most abundant in New England coastal waters and easiest to observe. Large schools gather in harbors and along beaches, making this the best time for identification practice.
seasonality.fall: Scup remain active and visible in coastal waters but begin preparing for their offshore migration as temperatures start to drop. Still commonly seen but in smaller numbers than summer.
seasonality.winter: Scup move to deeper offshore waters along the continental shelf and are rarely seen in typical coastal observation areas. They essentially disappear from accessible New England waters during this season.

funFact: Scup were so incredibly abundant in colonial New England that they were once used as fertilizer for crops when catches were too large to eat or sell — entire fields would be covered with these silvery fish to enrich the soil!
confusionNotes: Scup are often confused with other silvery fish like striped bass juveniles or black sea bass, but scup's deep, compressed oval body is much more pancake-like than the elongated bass species. Remember: scup are shaped like a silver dollar, bass are shaped like a torpedo.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse scup with 'scups' from video games — this is a real fish with deep New England roots! The scup fishery is one of America's oldest, with records dating back to 1800, and they were once the most abundant fish in colonial waters before overfishing in the 1990s.
compareHints: Scup are the only member of their genus in New England waters, but they're closely related to other porgies in the seabream family. Compared to other local porgies, scup have a more compressed, oval body shape and smaller mouth, while their relatives tend to be either more elongated or have larger, more prominent mouths. The deep, flattened profile is scup's signature feature among New England porgies.
